walkthroughs.body_html: E.G. Ravenstein (1885) derived 11 Laws of Migration from UK census data, still influential. Key claims: most migrants travel short distances; long-distance migrants head to major commercial cities; each migration current produces a counter-current; rural inhabitants migrate more than urban; women dominate short-distance moves; technology accelerates migration; economic motives dominate. His work pioneered modelling migration mathematically rather than describing it anecdotally.

Everett Lee reformulated migration as a function of factors at origin (negatives like unemployment, conflict; positives like family ties), destination (positives like jobs, safety; negatives like housing costs), intervening obstacles (distance, visas, smuggler fees, language), and personal factors (age, education, networks). Lee predicted migration is selective: not everyone moves equally, and selectivity rises with stronger negative push factors.

Contemporary scholars critique push-pull as overly mechanical. Network theory (Massey et al.) argues established migrants reduce costs and risks for new entrants, producing self-reinforcing flows (e.g. Mexico-US, Bangladesh-UK). Migration systems theory (Mabogunje) sees flows as feedback loops including remittances, return migration, and policy responses. Aspirations and capabilities frameworks (de Haas, 2021) integrate freedom and structural constraints.
